newsitem.title: USA: Tobacco stocks wait to exhale after bad market day.
newsitem.headline: Tobacco stocks wait to exhale after bad market day.

text.p: Tobacco stocks including industry leader Philip Morris Cos. Inc. plunged as much as 8 percent Thursday on rekindled worries about litigation and in an overall weak market.
On the New York Stock Exchange, shares of Philip Morris plunged $10.75 to close at $126. RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp dropped $2.875 to $33.25, Loews Corp. fell $6 to $104.375.
The Dow Jones industrial average fell 160.48 points, or 2.28 percent, to close at 6,878.89.
Two blows hit tobacco stocks Thursday.
Mississippi's highest court ruled that the first state Medicaid suit seeking to recoup health care costs of smokers can go to trial.
The Mississippi Supreme Court threw out challenges by Gov. Kirk Fordice and the tobacco industry that would have kept the $940 million case from proceeding to trial on June 2.
This is the first of 22 such suits filed by state attorneys generals across the country seeking to recoup Medicaid costs.

Secondly, Liggett Group Inc., a unit of Brook Group Ltd, was said to be preparing to expand its negotiated settlement of tobacco liability suits to dozens of those states, sources told Reuters Wednesday.

Liggett struck its landmark settlement in New Orleans a year ago to settle a federal class-action lawsuit. Any deal that expanded the settlement was seen as likely to pressure other tobacco firms to follow suit.
Brook Group shares rose 25 cents to $4.50.
Analysts noted that it was a nervous time for stockholders, watching court cases proceeding one by one.
"Over the next five months I would be looking for a little more volatility in the (tobacco stocks)," said Smith Barney analyst Martin Feldman.
But analysts repeated that the rate of earnings growth, the legal defences and already weak prices should soothe fears.
"The fundamentals of the business are extremely strong, Philip Morris is growing its earnings by about 18 percent (per year) and ... its defences are incredible," Feldman said.
No tobacco company has so far paid a cent in damages in a U.S. court, and the industry argues that long-standing health warnings on packs are a strong defence against most charges.

Paine Webber's Emanuel Goldman said the threat that Liggett would release industry documents that imply a higher degree of culpability by the industry in personal injuries was toothless, because the documents "are nothing."
"Even with those documents, you have to prove fraud at the highest level (of a tobacco company), and that's the hard part here," Goldman said.
